intro: You're looking for a discretionary trust will near you, which usually means you want more control over how your assets are passed on than a straightforward will allows. Perhaps you have a vulnerable family member, a complex family situation, or assets you want to protect for the longer term. A wills and probate specialist can explain how a discretionary trust will works and whether it suits your circumstances.
need_heading: What people searching for a discretionary trust will near me usually need
need_lead: Most people who search for a discretionary trust will near me are trying to balance flexibility, protection and family security.
needs: You want to provide for a child or adult who may not be able to manage money themselves, so trustees can decide how and when funds are used.
You have a family member who is receiving means-tested benefits and you want to avoid affecting their entitlement, while still helping them in the future.
You are worried about a beneficiary's creditors or a possible divorce, and you want the trust to protect assets from being lost outside the family.
You have a blended family and want to ensure your current partner is provided for while ultimately preserving assets for your children.
You want to leave a letter of wishes to guide your trustees on how you would like the trust to be used, without making it legally binding.
context_heading: One key thing to understand about discretionary trust wills
context: A discretionary trust will allows your trustees to decide how assets are used among a group of beneficiaries. This gives flexibility and protection, but trusts have their own tax rules, so it is important to understand the potential tax consequences. A specialist can explain how these rules apply to your situation.

Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors (regulated by the SRA) and chartered legal executives (regulated by CILEx) are regulated, insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman. Many specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly. When choosing a provider, ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and where your original will is stored. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when enquiring
tell: Mention that you are interested in a discretionary trust will and what you hope to achieve, such as protecting a vulnerable beneficiary or keeping assets in the family.
Describe your family circumstances, including any children from a previous relationship, a spouse or partner, or dependants with additional needs.
Explain whether any beneficiary receives means-tested benefits or has creditors, as this can affect how the trust is set up.
Say whether you already have a will and whether you want to update it or start afresh.
Confirm where you live, as the law differs across the UK, and whether you need advice on property or assets in another jurisdiction.
Let us know if you have a letter of wishes or any existing trust arrangements, so the specialist can take these into account.

faqs.q: Do I need a discretionary trust will if I have a vulnerable child?
faqs.a: A discretionary trust will can be useful for vulnerable beneficiaries because trustees can decide how assets are used for them over time. It can help ensure money is managed sensibly and protected from outside risks. A specialist can advise whether it is appropriate for your child's needs.

faqs.q: What is a letter of wishes and do I need one?
faqs.a: A letter of wishes is a non-binding document that guides your trustees on how you would like the trust to be used. It can be helpful for explaining your intentions, especially in complex family situations. It is not legally binding, but trustees will usually consider it.

Discretionary trusts have their own tax rules, including potential inheritance tax, income tax and capital gains tax implications. The rules can be complex and depend on the trust's assets and how it is managed. A wills and probate specialist can explain how these might apply to your situation.

faqs.q: Can I set up a discretionary trust will if I live in Scotland?
faqs.a: Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so a discretionary trust will may be treated differently. It is important to use an adviser who practises in Scotland and understands Scots law. iComply can introduce you to a suitable professional in your jurisdiction.
